cases.working_notes: Prioritize learned action tokenization, behavioral diversity, and faster action generation. The robot comparison distinguishes standalone task performance from sequential execution; it does not establish reduced overfitting. Table 3 appears to reverse conditional and unconditional headings, so use Table 7 for timing. Figure 5 task labels conflict with the stated ablation settings; avoid its extracted numbers. The entropy findings can be described from Section 4.3 without treating the extracted figure annotations as unambiguous entropy values. Trial-level uncertainty would be needed for inferential claims about the selected robot totals.
cases.abstract: We introduce Vector-Quantized Behavior Transformers (VQ-BeT), a method for learning multimodal continuous behaviors from uncurated demonstrations using learned action tokens instead of k-means action bins. Residual vector quantization encodes actions or action chunks as coarse and fine codes, which a transformer predicts from observation histories with optional goal conditioning. A continuous correction refines each decoded action, while token prediction generates actions in a single forward pass. In simulated manipulation and locomotion, VQ-BeT generally matches or exceeds the tested transformer and diffusion baselines in task performance and captures diverse behaviors in entropy measurements and rollouts; diffusion policies nevertheless perform better on unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush. A low-cost mobile manipulator provides a complementary test of sequential execution under controller noise. With all policies running fully closed-loop, VQ-BeT completes 19 of 30 two-phase trials, compared with 11 for an adapted DiffusionPolicy-T, while their single-phase results are close. Inference on the robot's onboard CPU takes 207.25 ms versus 5243.82 ms. Together, these comparisons support learned action tokenization as a way to combine behavioral diversity, sequential task performance, and faster action generation in the evaluated settings.
cases.results: The real-robot comparison separates standalone task execution from sequential behavior generation. Under fully closed-loop control on the low-cost mobile manipulator, VQ-BeT succeeds in 47/50 single-phase trials and the adapted DiffusionPolicy-T in 45/50, but their totals diverge on two-phase tasks: 19/30 versus 11/30. Thus, the larger advantage appears when policies must complete successive subtasks, rather than standalone tasks. VQ-BeT also closes the fridge and toaster in both orders, providing rollout evidence that successful behavior need not collapse to one sequence. Final success rates on each of four longer sequences are at least three times the diffusion baseline's. Onboard CPU inference is 207.25 ms for VQ-BeT versus 5243.82 ms for diffusion. These timings matter because controller noise prevented receding-horizon execution in this setup, requiring a new policy prediction at every step.

Final-checkpoint evaluations use 20 trials per method with shared initial conditions; training curves instead track noisy online episodes. cases.abstract: Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) uses a separately trained imitation policy to guide both online action selection and temporal-difference targets. At each state, an off-policy critic compares actions proposed by the imitation and reinforcement-learning policies; the same comparison supplies the bootstrap action during training. This preserves demonstrations as an active source of candidate actions without imposing a behavior-cloning regularizer on the learned policy. Keeping the policies separate also permits different visual architectures for imitation and reinforcement learning. Experiments with sparse task-completion rewards show faster learning than demonstration oversampling and regularized fine-tuning on Robomimic, while regularized fine-tuning performs similarly on simpler Meta-World tasks. Ablations find that removing either proposal mechanism reduces performance even with actor dropout, and that a shallow vision transformer favors online learning whereas ResNet-18 favors behavior cloning. On real robots using manual resets, 30 demonstrations, and 30,000 interaction steps for cloth hanging, IBRL achieves 85% success versus 65% for behavior cloning, 35% for regularized fine-tuning, and 15% for demonstration oversampling. These results support critic-mediated use of imitation for policy improvement under sparse rewards.
cases.results: In the real-world Hang task, IBRL improves beyond imitation where the two alternative demonstration-based RL methods fall below it. With 30 demonstrations and a matched budget of 30,000 interaction steps, IBRL reaches 85% evaluation success, compared with 65% for the reference behavior-cloning policy, 35% for regularized fine-tuning, and 15% for RLPD. These are evaluations of the final checkpoints over 20 trials per method with the same initial conditions, rather than success rates from noisy training rollouts. The 20-percentage-point gain over cloning supports policy improvement on deformable-cloth manipulation, not merely reproduction of demonstrated behavior. In the Robomimic Square ablations, removing either imitation-based action proposal or bootstrap proposal worsens performance despite retaining actor dropout; adding dropout to the baselines also leaves IBRL ahead. Together, the comparisons support using imitation actions in both interaction and value learning. The hardware protocol uses sparse success rewards and manual resets.
